items.title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.original_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_description: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/28/2026 - 16:09 Life insurers are AI. The next challenge is preparing for policyholders who use AI to understand, question and optimize their policies. November 5, 2026 Image Imagine the customer of a 20-year-old life insurance policy trying to figure out if it makes sense to surrender the policy. Do they call the insurance company first, hoping to talk to a knowledgeable agent? Probably not. They will upload the policy contract, riders and most recent statement to the AI assistant with a list of questions: What benefits would be lost by surrendering the policy? What happens to the outstanding loans? Are there other alternatives to surrendering the policy? Which policy provisions are the most important to consider before deciding? This AI might be right, or might be partly right, or might be very wrong. But what is becoming abundantly clear is that this customer arrives at their insurer with a level of analysis and a body of knowledge that once cost time, or cost money, or both. This leads me back to the question insurers have been asking for years about how AI will change what we do: underwriting, servicing, operations, all inside the enterprise. So what happens when the policyholder is AI-enabled as well? The information gap is starting to change The Society of Actuaries Research Institute is now seeking research on policyholder behavior in the artificial intelligence era. According to the proposal request, it is possible for consumers to use AI to understand a policy's provisions better to improve their premiums, loans and withdrawals, and claims through improved product features. That isn't proof that AI has changed lapse rates, loan behavior, or benefit usage yet. It's on the research agenda. The difference is significant. But the formal asking of such questions by the actuarial community indicates that consumer AI requires attention before the results become apparent in experience studies. Up until recently, this has created a bit of a predicament: an insurer has product specialists, actuaries, underwriters, policy administration systems, and decades of institutional knowledge; a policyholder has a lengthy contract written in technical language and maybe the occasion to review it a couple of times. Generative AI won't remove that imbalance entirely, but it certainly lowers the cost of asking sophisticated questions about a complex contract. That alone changes the dynamic of that interaction. A long-lived contract can meet a very different customer Life insurance is unique because the contract could go on for decades, and the technology available to the user would be different from the present one. A policy issued in the age of paper statements and telephone calls may one day be managed by a consumer carrying a persistence layer of AI that summarizes documents, compares alternatives, remembers every previous conversation, and prepares detailed questions before every interaction. The policy's bones haven't altered one bit. But a policyholder's ability to kick the tires and check them out has. All this matters because many decisions and actions can occur throughout the lifecycle of a single life insurance policy: premium payment policy, loans, withdrawals, changes of beneficiary, conversion, surrender, and more. By making those decisions easier to understand and execute throughout the life of the product, there's no guarantee that customer behavior in the future will continue to be like the historical behaviors that informed product assumptions. Policyholder behavior may become an AI issue SOA's current research request explicitly identifies potential effects on lapses, loans, withdrawals, and benefit usage. A separate 2026 SOA call for essays on AI and the potential for antiselection in life insurance distribution asks whether AI could help applicants or intermediaries anticipate underwriting outcomes, compare carriers, select underwriting pathways and apply sophisticated placement strategies at greater scale. Once more, these are questions under investigation, not established outcomes. But, one thing appears clear: certain presumptions in life insurance are based on how people behave. Making it easier to evaluate the timing and consequences of a lapse, loan, withdrawal, conversion, surrender, or benefit election changes behavior in ways that historical behavior doesn't predict. The negative reaction to that realization is to predict material disruption. The right reaction is to begin measuring whether AI-assisted behavior is emerging, where it's concentrated, and if it's big enough to matter. From a more strategic perspective, for our actuarial and product teams, consumer AI could one day become another behavioral variable to study, rather than just a way to service customers better. AI-enabled policyholders can also be good for insurers This should not be framed only as a new risk. When a customer understands the policy, it allows them to ask the right questions, know what benefits they have, prepare the right documents, and know what decision they are making. Beneficiaries will use AI to organize materials for a claim, point out relevant policy language, and understand what the insurer is asking for. A policyholder who walks up to the window to service their policy will know the difference between a loan, withdrawal, and a surrender. This is consistent with the financial services research. In July 2026, LIMRA reported that AI is increasingly being studied not only as a tool that assists advisors but as a potential source of analysis and financial guidance directly to consumers. While more knowledgeable buyers are good for insurers, they also bring heightened expectations. A customer who has just received an instantaneous explanation of a policy provision may be less patient about waiting for days to get a generic response from a service agent. The customer's AI is not the insurer's AI Yet there is a boundary—the policyholder's AI is outside of the insurer's control. The model was not chosen, trained, fed, or even provided with its system prompt by the insurer. Your AI could be reading an outdated contract, skipping an endorsement, not grasping a rider, getting guaranteed vs. non-guaranteed values mixed up, or just making up a provision out of whole cloth that does not exist. The assertion could be false, or at least inaccurate. The enterprise response is to make verifying what the authoritative policy information says more accessible. Suppose a customer says, "My AI says this rider gives me a different option." It should be easy for a service person to say, "Let's review what your current contract and its effective endorsements, transaction history, and applicable rules say about this." The more external AI becomes part of customer decision-making, the more valuable clear, accessible, and authoritative policy context becomes. Soon, the customer may send the AI instead The next step is not difficult to imagine: the policyholder does not merely use AI before contacting the insurer. The AI contacts the insurer. That scenario is beginning to appear in insurance discussions already. An October 2026 Insurance Thought Leadership article described consumer AI agents calling insurers and other businesses on behalf of users. At the same time, NIST is developing work around identity and authorization for software and AI agents as agent-to-agent interactions move from concept toward practical infrastructure. This brings us to a much bigger question for life insurers: what if a chatbot does work? How would your service channel know that it's talking to software working for a policyholder? What data could be returned through that channel? What happens when a customer AI and your system don't agree on a policy provision? When does it become important to switch the interaction over to a person? There's nothing in those two scenarios that necessitates banning the use of AI in customer service. It just means that we, as users of these services, will need to create different channels for them to go through. Build policyholder AI readiness Insurers do not need to predict exactly how fast consumer agents will mature, but they do need to prepare for the direction of travel. First, make authoritative policy context easier to retrieve and explain. A policyholder's AI will only be as useful as the documents and information it can access. Clear digital contracts, current riders, transaction history, and understandable definitions reduce the chance that outside AI starts from incomplete context. Next, test servicing journeys with customers being assisted by AI in mind. When customers arrive having 10 specific questions, they should not follow the same process as someone who has only general questions. Third, watch how behavior changes. Teams — actuarial, product, servicing — that rely on lapses, loans, withdrawals, conversions, benefit usage, and channel usage need to understand what constitutes a significant deviation. We want to avoid blaming AI if another force is at work. The goal is to build evidence that indicates that AI is a cause before rewriting our assumptions about behavior. Fourth, prepare digital channels for external agents. Identity, consent, disclosure and escalation will become practical. We do not want to automatically trust an outside agent. We do want to ensure legitimate customer assistance can reach us and not diminish customer protection. The next AI transformation may happen outside the insurer When asked about the insurance AI strategy, carriers invariably identify the same things: automated underwriting, automated servicing, automated claims, automated document processing, and automated decision support. However, when it comes to the impact of artificial intelligence on enhancing service innovation, customer capabilities are also affected. The increased understanding could allow them to compare things to other products, which could open them up to asking difficult questions. However, what I think we have not talked about and probably is an elephant in the room is that insurers are not going to be in control of all this. They can only prepare for it. Will the next phase of life insurance AI be defined by how intelligent the insurer becomes? Or by what happens when the policyholder becomes intelligent at machine speed? Bhargavi Vepuri

items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

items.rss_description: Demo: AI Agent for P&C Claims Coverage Verification Insurtech in Action: The ITL Demos RyanMeyer Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:42 ScienceSoft's agentic solution matches P&C claim details against policy documents and delivers evidence-backed coverage conclusions in minutes while keeping adjusters in control of final decisions November 4, 2026 Watch Our Demo: Why We Are the Right Solution For Your Needs ScienceSoft's AI Agent for P&C Claims Coverage Verification adapts to your existing operations and technology landscape rather than forcing you to work around the software. Comes ready for coverage verification. The agent can automate the end-to-end workflow out of the box, from policy research and coverage analysis to evidence-backed memos and reservation of rights letters. Fits your claims processes and rules. ScienceSoft can customize the agent's verification logic, workflows, and outputs to reflect your coverage policies, authority levels, and claims handling practices. Lets you set the boundaries for AI. Built-in controls allow you to define which findings require human review, when the agent should escalate a case, and how AI-generated conclusions are validated. Works with your existing systems. The solution can integrate with commercial claims platforms and legacy applications without limiting your technology stack. You can deploy it in your cloud or on-premises environment. Watch the demo to see the agent verify coverage for a homeowners hail damage claim. Main Benefits of Our Product: Faster coverage verification. Bert Ji had joined Embassy Asset Management in February 2026, becoming one of the portfolio managers for the Ambassador Fund strategy and the insurance-linked securities portfolios managed by the firm. Ji had previously spent more than eight years working at specialist ILS investment manager Nephila Capital, becoming Head of Portfolio Management at that firm in 2021. He had previously spent five years at reinsurance group Validus Re, working in catastrophe risk modelling and analysis. We understand that MacGillivray departed from Embassy in October, having spent three years with the company. He joined Embassy in September 2023 , having previously worked for ILS specialist manager Tangency Capital which had been the sub-advisor of the Ambassador Fund when it launched. Ji had supported MacGillivray in the portfolio management of the cat bond focused fund strategy since joining Embassy earlier this year. Now, he takes over the lead Portfolio Manager role and is primarily responsible for the day-to-day management of the Ambassador Fund’s portfolio, assisted by other members of the investment team of Embassy Asset Management LP. As we’d reported in September , the Ambassador cat bond fund strategy reached a new milestone with its net assets under management practically at $1 billion. The cat bond fund’s AUM has now surpassed the $1 billion milestone, being at a reported $1.03 billion as of the end of October 2026. items.extracted_text: Democrats Planning Flood of AI Bills When They Take Control of Congress Article 0 Comments Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of the U.S. Congress in January, lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates said. The plans would mark a sharp shift from the Republican-led Congress, where lawmakers largely focused on promoting AI development and declined to pass legislation restricting aspects of the technology at a time when voters turned against the rapid development of data centers and their extensive power needs. Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply Democrats plan on introducing bills aimed at shielding consumers from rising electricity costs tied to data centers, requiring independent testing of advanced AI systems and clarifying when AI companies can be held liable for harm caused by their products, they said. Any legislation would face steep odds while Republican President Donald Trump remains in the White House, as he has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology. On Friday, Trump said he would work with U.S. states that “want to become RICH” by embracing AI, without offering details. But Democratic lawmakers and outside advocates said control of congressional committees would give the party a platform to advance proposals, compel testimony from industry leaders and build support for action if AI systems cause real-world harm. Representative Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat and chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, already said this week that AI executives should be called to testify under oath. Related: Google AI in School Triggered Teen’s Mental Health Crisis, Lawsuit Says Federal government restrictions on AI development could hurt the industry’s profits if they slow the release of new models or prompt the companies to change how their AI tools perform to address concerns that their products are harming people. Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress will slow AI development, and also on fears that the massive capital expense on building out AI will not yield sufficient returns. Stocks on Friday extended their slide in both Europe and Asia following the rout, though Wall Street futures pointed to a modest bounce for the Nasdaq later on Friday. Multiple Bills Likely Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Thursday at an event in Washington that protecting consumers from higher energy costs linked to the rapid expansion of data centers would be among his priorities next year. Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, one of the Democratic Party’s leading voices on AI policy, plans to push legislation requiring independent experts to evaluate leading AI models against safety standards, said Francis Grubar, her deputy chief of staff. Trahan will also pursue legislation clarifying that companies can be held responsible when AI systems act in harmful ways, he said. Representative Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat from California who is seeking to chair the House Science Committee, said Democrats would focus on developing “responsible regulations for AI while also fostering innovation.” Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who won a Senate seat on Tuesday, called during his campaign for an independent agency to oversee AI regulation with the power to police tech companies developing the technology. Public concern about AI is already high. Most U.S. voters think Trump’s administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new regulations for the technology, according to a Reuters poll published in October. A crisis could build enough support to overcome presidential opposition to AI regulation, said Ed Mills, who manages policy research at Raymond James. “The probability of legislation is much higher than people anticipate,” he said. Congress can override a presidential veto with the backing of two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers. Democrats could also try to insert AI regulation into routine bills that must pass Congress each year, Mills said. Democrats also plan to use their new authority to intensify scrutiny of the industry’s most powerful companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Lofgren and other Democratic House committee leaders in October asked OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Alphabet’s Google and SpaceX to detail their security practices and report instances of their AI tools taking actions that their designers did not intend. items.extracted_text: Home-Renovation Expense Keeps Rising as Companies Pass on Costs Article 0 Comments Households squeezed by high grocery and gas prices are facing another hit: rising costs for home repairs and upgrades. The cost of repairing or remodeling a home has risen steadily through October, with higher oil and energy prices, along with elevated interest rates stemming from the Iran conflict, pushing prices up. In the three months through June, it rose at the fastest quarterly pace since October 2024, according to insurance data analytics provider Verisk. Repair bills could climb further as manufacturers of paint, plumbing fixtures, appliances and air conditioners — which already lifted prices last year due to tariffs — push through another round of increases to offset higher materials and freight costs. “Just to put it in perspective, this quarter was the most significant inflationary period that we’ve experienced since mid-2022,” Armstrong World Industries Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mark Hershey said on an earnings call. The ceiling maker raised prices in November, noting its freight costs had risen about 20% from a year earlier. Paint producer Sherwin-Williams Co. raised prices 8% in September and hasn’t ruled out further hikes. Pool Corp. did the same, as did HVAC manufacturer Carrier Global Corp., citing higher steel, copper, aluminum and freight costs, expecting inflationary pressures to persist into 2027. Whirlpool Corp., which sells the KitchenAid, Maytag and inSinkErator labels alongside its namesake brand, will boost U.S. prices by 7% in December. “We will have meaningful inflation to address in 2027,” construction tools make Stanley Black & Decker Inc. Chief Financial Officer Patrick Hallinan said on an earnings call. “We plan to do so with productivity measures and pricing actions, with a price increase likely around the turn of the year.” The ability to pass along higher costs to consumers depends on the product, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Drew Reading. Homeowners are less able to avoid repairs and maintenance, though they may trade down on items like faucets or toilets. That silver lining may put a floor under earnings. Roofing maker Carlisle Cos Inc. expects current pricing to become a tailwind as costs normalize in 2027. Price increases are expected to catch up with rising costs by the end of 2026. So far, higher prices have not hurt demand or prompted more pre-buying, CEO Christian Koch said in an earnings call. Masco Corp., which makes faucets under brands including Hansgrohe, credited pricing with partly helping drive a 13% adjusted operating profit increase in the third quarter. Regarding potential price hikes in 2027, CEO Jonathon Nudi said pricing is the “last lever we pull.” Existing price increases largely reflect earlier tariff and input-cost mitigation, Reading said. Accelerating copper, oil-based materials and freight costs create the potential need for Masco to raise prices in 2027. items.extracted_text: Brokerslink launches ekko platform to boost multinational programme solutions - Commercial Risk Carla Alves, Brokerslink Brokerslink has launched a new digital platform to help its members better deliver for customers by more easily accessing and sharing the network’s expertise to create broader, global solutions for multinational firms. It believes that ekko will help Brokerslink compete with the global broking firms on big multinational programmes. The new ekko tool will support collaboration and improve coordination between Brokerslink partners and affiliates, the network said on launching the platform at its annual conference in Istanbul. Ekko is complemented by a redesigned Brokerslink website to provide multinational clients, risk managers, insurers and other market stakeholders with clearer visibility of the network’s geographic presence, specialist capabilities and services. Ekko includes “Deal Rooms” to help Brokerslink members collaborate on specific client needs and opportunities. A marketplace function allows each member to know exactly what others offer across the world to find the best solution for risk managers and insurance buyers. “Ekko represents a fundamental change in how we manage and develop our global network. Accurate data and the right technology will allow us to make better decisions, plan more effectively and identify opportunities that were previously difficult to capture. For our partners and affiliates, ekko creates practical tools to connect expertise, strengthen collaboration and generate business. Our ambition is to translate the strength of our network into measurable value for our members and their clients,” said Carla Alves, who led the ekko project and is director of marketing and operations at Brokerslink. She told Commercial Risk that the platform will improve Brokerslink’s ability to tackle multinational solutions for big clients. “Our brokers will be able to offer their clients capacities, solutions and services faster and more easily wherever they are in the world. We have all the capabilities inside the network in Singapore, Hong Kong, Madrid, London, New York or wherever. Members will now be able to offer all this more quickly to their clients to service the multinational programmes they need,” she said. “What we hope to achieve with this is to make the connections more visible to the network, using specialty brokers or specialty companies within ekko. So our brokers will be able to deliver a different value proposition to their multinational clients than before,” added Alves. Ekko is based on a Salesforce-based CRM and has a dedicated mobile application that its members can access. It replaces Brokerslink’s previous member system, Agora, and represents the first phase of a broader technology programme, with further developments planned for 2027. “The deal rooms will allow every single platform user to go in and search for a solution and make a connection with a specific market and create a closed deal room, where they can share information…it will help deliver expertise beyond existing connections to find the right partner, all the way through to closing the deal,” explained Anna Collette, business development and partnerships director at Brokerslink. “The marketplace is about making it easier to access solutions that our wholesalers and specialists can provide. Our members can now use ekko to search for expertise on a particular risk, person or solution to deliver insurance or risk management advice,” she added. Alves said the success of ekko will not be measured by the launch itself but by how Brokerslink members use the tool to deliver for clients. “We now have the machine, but what is inside will be provided by you and the data,” she told Brokerslink members in Istanbul. “The more you will give, the more you will get…explore, use and contribute with your knowledge.” Ben Norris November 6, 2026 Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit Messenger Messenger WhatsApp Share via Email Print Read Next GRM Insurance November 6, 2026 Liberty Mutual Q3 profit falls 7% as catastrophe losses rise GRM Insurance November 6, 2026 Amiga Specialty expands commercial professional indemnity capacity Risk Management November 6, 2026 Risk management leaders warn against overreliance on insurance to build resilience GRM People Moves November 5, 2026 SRS Altitude appoints head of ART for North America GRM People Moves November 5, 2026 HDI Global UK & Ireland names head of political violence and terrorism November 6, 2026 Liberty Mutual Q3 profit falls 7% as catastrophe losses rise November 6, 2026 Amiga Specialty expands commercial professional indemnity capacity November 6, 2026 Risk management leaders warn against overreliance on insurance to build resilience November 5, 2026 SRS Altitude appoints head of ART for North America November 5, 2026 HDI Global UK & Ireland names head of political violence and terrorism Related Articles Allianz Commercial announces new Lloyd’s syndicate November 5, 2026 Swiss Re P&C revenues decline in competitive market November 5, 2026 Lori Goltermann leaves Aon for new Swiss Re Corporate Solutions role November 5, 2026 Aon expands follow-form facility to 35% for 2027 November 5, 2026 Back to top button Close Close Log In

items.title: Investors settle with KPMG over Silicon Valley Bank collapse
items.original_title: Investors settle with KPMG over Silicon Valley Bank collapse
items.rss_title: Investors settle with KPMG over Silicon Valley Bank collapse
items.rss_description: Investors involved in a class action lawsuit over the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank have reached a $224.5 million settlement with external auditor KPMG, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund said on Friday.
items.extracted_text: KPMG said the settlement was not an admission of wrongdoing and that it stood by its work. SVB’s collapse in March 2023 triggered the worst banking shock since the 2008 global financial crisis, affecting bank stocks globally. The Norwegian fund later said the case raised significant concerns regarding the integrity of the public markets, the governance of large financial institutions and the interests of the investor community more broadly. “The settlement is an important first step toward recovering investor losses from one of the largest bank failures in U.S. history,” Nicolai Tangen, CEO of the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund, said in a statement. “We continue to stand by our audits of Silicon Valley Bank, and we are proud of our audit quality track record. This settlement is a strategic decision to move forward as a business. It is not an admission of any wrongdoing,” a KPMG US spokesperson said in a written statement. The class action case continues against other defendants, the Norwegian fund said. The fund, which invests Norway’s surplus oil and gas revenue abroad, is the world’s biggest single stock market investor, owning some 1.5% of all globally listed shares with stakes in more than 7,000 companies. It held a 1% stake in SVB at the end of 2022, valued at $137.9 million, according to data on the fund’s website. items.extracted_text: Vantage Partnership Capital (AdVantage) drives $15m income for Howard Hughes in Q3 2026 - Artemis.bm Vantage Partnership Capital (AdVantage) drives $15m income for Howard Hughes in Q3 2026 - Artemis.bm Vantage Partnership Capital (AdVantage) drives $15m income for Howard Hughes in Q3 2026 6th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Vantage Risk’s third-party reinsurance capital and investments platform has again delivered higher fee income to the benefit of its now owner, Bill Ackman linked Howard Hughes Holdings, with $13 million of fee income generated by its insurance-linked securities style partnerships with investors in Q3 2026 and $15 million of total net income from the ILS activities. It takes year-to-date fee income earned by the Vantage Partnership Capital team, operating its business through the AdVantage platform of companies, to $47 million. The third-quarter 2026 net fee income from the ILS and reinsurance investment operations of $13 million is up $4 million on the prior-year period, as seemingly the AdVantage strategies have benefited from the relatively benign environment for major catastrophe losses. In the prior quarter, Vantage’s third-party reinsurance capital platform generated $23 million of fee income from its ILS style partnerships with investors in the second-quarter of 2026 . For the 2026 calendar year, the Vantage Partnership Capital business, operating through the AdVantage structures, has a higher $1.6 billion of capital to deploy than it did in 2025. Fee income is now running higher, through both second and third quarters in 2026, but as well as the additional capital under management, the AdVantage structures have also been benefiting from variable fee income inputs. At $47 million of net fee income for the first nine months of 2026, it’s a meaningful increase from the -$5 million that fee income sat at after 9-month 2025 (presumably due to catastrophe loss events such as the Los Angeles wildfires earlier that year). Howard Hughes Holding stated that Q3 2026 fee income for AdVantage was, “resulting from the continued positive outcomes for recent property catastrophe business written in this structure.” Marc Grandisson, the former Arch Capital CEO who joined the Howard Hughes Holdings Board of Directors this year, commented during an earnings call today, “Net fee income was $13 million in the quarter, up from $9 million, and is $47 million year to date, versus the loss last year. “This comes from our AdVantage ILS structure and reflects strong outcomes on recent property cat business we wrote for third-party partners.” Vantage Risk itself reported no catastrophe losses for the third-quarter and $4 million of favorable prior-year development, which may be a factor in higher variable fee income flowing to AdVantage in the period, although we cannot be certain as the reason for the variability was not disclosed. On top of the fee income from the ILS business, Howard Hughes Holdings also reported $4 million of underwriting income from the AdVantage strategies in Q3 2026, taking total pre-tax income to $17 million and net income to $15 million after $2 million of earnings for non-controlling interests (presumably capital providers). The AdVantage ILS related activities deliver an asset-light stream of fee income for Howard Hughes, while also increasing Vantage’s underwriting capacity at the same time and enabling it to optimise its portfolios, with the help of third-party capital investors. items.extracted_text: Flooding Inundates North Georgia but Few Had Flood Coverage, Agents Say Article 0 Comments Insurance agents in north Georgia are reporting widespread damage after record flooding hit the area Thursday, Nov. 5. “It’s devastating. I have cried and prayed and cried and prayed,” said an agent who answered the phone at Appalachian Insurance Services in Blue Ridge, Georgia, near the Tennessee line. Some property owners carried flood insurance but most did not, because the town has not seen flooding of this scale in decades, agents said. Cody Webb, an agent at Mountain Insurance in Blue Ridge, said his office escaped damage. Multiple policyholders have contacted the agency, but most did not have flood coverage. “People were expecting rain, but no one expected this much,” Webb said Friday morning. As much as 10 inches of rain fell overnight Wednesday between Blue Ridge and Ellijay, and runoff quickly overwhelmed streams and rivers in the area, the Associated Press and other news sites reported. The storms dumped rain all across the mountainous area that drains into the Toccoa River that flows between Copperhill, Tennessee, and McCaysville, Georgia. The Toccoa flows into the Ocoee River, where the Tennessee Valley Authority said it was managing high water levels at three hydroelectric dams, AP reported. The Toccoa reached a record high Thursday morning at 18 feet, a river guage showed, and the waters completely submerged some homes and buildings, AP and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. At least 57 people were rescued before the floodwaters began to recede, the Fannin County Emergency Management Agency in Georgia said. It’s the second flood in McCaysville this year. In August, a flash flood from mountain rains and runoff damaged the police station and post office as well as a number of homes and businesses. The renovated police station reopened just last week, AP noted. After two floods in three months, “I don’t know what God is trying to tell me,” Police Chief Michael Early told AP. Shelby Patterson, a commercial lines agent at The Insurance Mart, who lives in McCaysville, said at least four policyholders had reported heavy damage from the flood. Two of them had flood coverage. “But two only had homeowners’ insurance, and they are freaking out,” Patterson said. The flooding brought loads of mud and silt into buildings in McCaysville and Blue Ridge. After the waters receded, residents were seen carrying bucket after bucket of mud out of homes, she noted. Another resident’s propane tank exploded, compounding damage left by floodwaters, Patterson noted. Dickey McCay Insurance agency in Copperhill, just across the river, was closed Friday due to the flooding. A voice mail directed policyholders to call a claims-handling phone number or to report claims to their carriers. Ironically, one adjuster firm, All American Public Adjusters, has offices in McCaysville. But the manager was in Pensacola, Florida, still working wind claims from Hurricane Isaias, which hit the Pensacola area Oct. 9. Topics Agencies Flood Georgia Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Blackstone, Aon Set Up Lloyd’s Vehicle in Latest Insurance Push Article 0 Comments Blackstone Inc. has set up a Lloyd’s of London syndicate with broker Aon Plc, as the world’s largest alternative asset manager muscles further into the insurance sector. Called Cortina, the syndicate will provide capital to back reinsurance contracts, according to a statement on Friday. The vehicle will take a 3% share of Aon-arranged contracts that cover insurers’ property portfolios once catastrophe losses exceed an agreed threshold, and 5% of all other eligible reinsurance deals facilitated by Aon. Insurance group QBE will be responsible for the syndicate’s underwriting and governance. The partnership “will broaden the pools of capital available to the reinsurance market, expanding capacity and strengthening resilience across market cycles,” said Blackstone President and Chief Operating Officer Jon Gray. While life insurance has long been a hunting ground for alternative asset managers like Blackstone, they are now increasingly pushing into property-and-casualty, or P&C, insurance. Alternative asset managers are drawn to the sector as gains and losses tend to be uncorrelated with wider financial markets. Insurers profit by collecting more in premiums than they pay out for claims, and by investing the premiums. P&C insurers and reinsurers generated an average 17% return on equity in 2025 after years of price increases, according to Aon, though global commercial insurance rates have fallen in recent quarters. Last year, Allianz SE and Oaktree Capital Management set up a reinsurance syndicate at Lloyd’s, the world’s biggest hub for commercial and specialty risk. Blackstone already backs a Lloyd’s reinsurance syndicate that takes on part of American International Group Inc.’s risks. In 2025, Blackstone said it will also back a new Lloyd’s syndicate that’s going to be run by Bermuda-based insurance underwriter The Fidelis Partnership. “As risks grow in scale and complexity, clients are looking for effective risk transfer solutions that consider all forms of available capital,” Aon Chief Executive Officer Greg Case said. Cortina plans to begin underwriting from Jan. 1, subject to final Lloyd’s approval. items.title: No relief for ‘The Pitt’ lawsuit
items.original_title: No relief for ‘The Pitt’ lawsuit
items.rss_title: No relief for ‘The Pitt’ lawsuit
items.rss_description: The legal drama surrounding two popular television medical dramas isn’t ready for discharge after a California appeals court ruled Wednesday that the estate of “ER” co-creator Michael Crichton can pursue its lawsuit alleging HBO’s “The Pitt” is an unauthorized reboot of the long-running hospital series.
items.extracted_text: Sherri Crichton, who oversees her late husband’s estate, sued Warner Bros. Television and the creators of “The Pitt” in 2024, alleging they developed the new series without obtaining permission required under a 1994 agreement. Mr. Crichton, who died in 2008, helped create “ER,” which aired on NBC from 1994 to 2009. Warner Bros. sought to dismiss the lawsuit under California’s anti-SLAPP law, which protects against lawsuits targeting free speech. A lower court rejected that effort, and a three-judge appellate panel upheld the decision, finding enough similarities between the two programs to let the case proceed, NBC News reported Thursday. Both shows follow emergency room doctors navigating medical crises and personal relationships, although “ER” was set in Chicago and “The Pitt” takes place in Pittsburgh. “The Pitt” lead actor Noah Wyle recently acknowledged that an “ER” reboot had initially been considered but said the creative team ultimately developed a separate series. The ruling did not diagnose whether “The Pitt” infringed Ms. Crichton’s rights. It allows the estate’s lawsuit to proceed. items.extracted_text: Aon and Blackstone funds launch Cortina, a new Lloyd's syndicate offering efficient reinsurance - Artemis.bm Aon and Blackstone funds launch Cortina, a new Lloyd's syndicate offering efficient reinsurance - Artemis.bm Aon and Blackstone funds launch Cortina, a new Lloyd’s syndicate offering efficient reinsurance 6th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Aon’s agreement with Blackstone over the much-discussed reinsurance facility at Lloyd’s named Cortina was signed this week and now the parties have announced its launch, while the London Bridge 2 insurance-linked securities structure appears to have been utilised in the funding of the new syndicate. We had been told the Cortina transaction effectively closed late Wednesday this week, after contractual agreements were approved and signed among the parties involved. Sources have said the agreement covers somewhere around $1.6 billion of premiums, while funding had been mooted at around the $500 million level. Now, Aon and Blackstone have formally announced the launch of the Cortina syndicate 1956 at Lloyd’s, revealing that the London Bridge 2 ILS structure was part of the initiative. The structure is designed to offer efficient long-term reinsurance capacity to Aon’s clients, while they will also benefit from a client dividend. Cortina syndicate 1956 is expected to begin underwriting from January 1st 2027 adopting a lead/follow approach, subject to final approval from Lloyd’s, while QBE will be managing agent of the syndicate and be responsible for the syndicate’s underwriting and governance. “As risks grow in scale and complexity, clients are looking for effective risk transfer solutions that consider all forms of available capital,” explained Greg Case, President and CEO, Aon. “Cortina is bringing additional, long-term capital through Blackstone together with QBE’s expertise and the strength of Lloyd’s to expand the market’s capacity to take risk, help close protection gaps and enable greater resilience, investment and growth.” “The partnership with Aon and QBE will broaden the pools of capital available to the reinsurance market, expanding capacity and strengthening resilience across market cycles,” added Jon Gray, President and Chief Operating Officer, Blackstone. “We remain strong supporters of continued innovation at Lloyd’s and are long-term investors in the sector. This partnership will help meet clients’ evolving needs while supporting the market’s long-term growth.” “Cortina is a first-of-its-kind model for reinsurance capacity at Lloyd’s,” Jason Harris, QBE International CEO said. “As managing agent, we bring deep, specialist underwriting expertise and our leading Lloyd’s capability to a syndicate that combines long-term institutional capital with stable, disciplined reinsurance capacity. It also gives us the opportunity to further grow our business through an innovative model. For QBE Re, the strategy remains unchanged: a continued focus on building long-term partnerships.” “Lloyd’s takes pride in being a market of firsts and in being the most capital-efficient marketplace in the world to connect capital to insurance risk,” commented Patrick Tiernan, Chief Executive, Lloyd’s. “By structuring this transaction at Lloyd’s, we see the marriage of new long-term capital through our London Bridge 2 framework, with the highest underwriting and oversight standards to create long term value for clients, investors and the marketplace. This is total innovation in action.” QBE is already partnered as a lead with Aon on its Client Treaty facility at Lloyd’s, which was renewed earlier this week with an expanded remit to provide 35% co-insurance of eligible business placed through Aon’s Global Broking Centre and facultative reinsurance business in the market for 2027 , an increase from 28.5% co-insurance in 2026. Cortina is designed to bring institutional third-party capital to support reinsurance of a meaningful slice of Aon’s brokered book in the market. Aon said the Cortina syndicate will offer following capacity on all eligible treaties, subject to a framework. This will include following lines of 3% on property catastrophe treaty business and 5% on other treaty lines. Aon’s CEO Greg Case has referred to Cortina a number of times recently, explaining at a KBW conference that the structure will enable Blackstone to participate in a broad portfolio of risks through a Lloyd’s syndicate. As Aon has established follow-capacity in that market for some year’s now, through its Aon Client Treaty, it’s likely the follow-lines will be originated, underwritten and delivered to Cortina in a similar manner. Cortina has stimulated quite the debate in the reinsurance market, with some questioning the need for more capacity in the market at this time of high competition and softening rates. At Lloyd’s itself, it appears to have perhaps been a contributor to the market issuing recent guidance on its expectations for any broker-originated reinsurance structures and facilities , a strategy that Lloyd’s said is likely to see increasing demand given capital’s interest in accessing the marketplace. Ultimately, Cortina demonstrates the appetite of major institutional investors to access returns of the reinsurance business in the most efficient manner possible. By gaining access to a slice of perhaps the biggest brokered book around and the agreement now said to be signed, it seems Blackstone has secured another route to expand on its insurance investments in the Lloyd’s market. Previously, just in the last year, we’ve seen Blackstone partner with The Fidelis Partnership on Syndicate 2126 , while also partnering with AIG on Syndicate 2479 , which was that insurer’s second such vehicle after the also Blackstone-partnered Syndicate 2478 . Cortina will expand access to reinsurance-linked returns via Lloyd’s for the asset manager and its investors, while also expanding the increasingly important role of institutional capital in the Lloyd’s marketplace. items.extracted_text: SafePoint adds another $100m+ layer to its catastrophe bond with Nature Coast Re 2026-4 - Artemis.bm SafePoint adds another $100m+ layer to its catastrophe bond with Nature Coast Re 2026-4 - Artemis.bm SafePoint adds another $100m+ layer to its catastrophe bond with Nature Coast Re 2026-4 6th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans In a clear display of the attractive catastrophe bond market conditions sponsors are experiencing, SafePoint Insurance Company is back to add another $100 million or more layer of reinsurance protection to its recently priced indemnity deal, with a Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-4) issuance now being offered to investors, Artemis understands. As we’ve been reporting, SafePoint successfully priced and secured its largest catastrophe bond ever, with the $650 million Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) . That indemnity and per-occurrence cat bond features two tranches of notes, providing named storm reinsurance protection to the insurer and its reciprocal exchanges, but now SafePoint is back to add a third that sits above them. In addition, SafePoint is already in the market with a new annual aggregate industry-loss triggered cat bond as well, targeting another $100 million through an Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 transaction. Which means, if the new deals are successful, SafePoint could end up securing $850 million or more in broad-scope cat bond backed reinsurance from the capital markets in just the space of a few weeks. It’s all the more notable given SafePoint has never been a company to simply sponsor cat bonds for the sake of it, they have always had to make economic sense to its management team. So, the fact SafePoint is returning again to further extend on its new cat bond coverage, should deliver a strong signal to any potential cat bond sponsors watching on, that market conditions are very attractive right now and multi-year reinsurance can be locked in at attractive rates in the cat bond market. Onto the new cat bond deal that SafePoint is now sponsoring, which is really an extension to the just priced $650 million Nature Coast Re 2026-2 . Nature Coast Re Ltd. is offering investors a single tranches of Series 2026-4 Class AAA catastrophe bond notes that will be sold to investors to provide the collateral to fully-support an underlying reinsurance agreement. The reinsurance agreement will protect SafePoint Insurance Company itself and the two reciprocal exchanges it operates, the Louisiana focused Cajun Underwriters Reciprocal Exchange entity, and the Florida homeowner and business owner focused Manatee Insurance Exchange. These Nature Coast Re 2026-4 cat bond notes will provide fully-collateralized reinsurance protection covering losses from named storms across the states of Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, the same as the Series 2026-2 notes. The coverage tracks the same as well, being on an indemnity and per-occurrence trigger basis and the reinsurance will run across a four-year period from December 1st, again the same as the Series 2026-2 notes. The only difference to the two tranches of Series 2026-2 notes, with these new Series 2026-4 notes, is the attachment level and so how risky they are. These Nature Coast Re 2026-4 cat bond notes are more remote in terms of their risk and we’re told are designed to sit at the top of the tower, above the two tranches of the 2026-2 issuance. The currently $100 million tranche of Series 2026-4 Class AAA notes have an attachment point of $300 million, taking a share of losses up to exhaustion at $900 million, sources told us, giving room for the issuance to be upsized from the initial target, should SafePoint elect to. The $100 million of Series 2026-4 Class AAA notes that Nature Coast Re is offering come with an initial attachment probability of 0.6%, an initial base expected loss of 0.46% and are being offered to investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 3% and 3.5%, we understand. That price guidance seems aligned with t he recently priced 2026-2 indemnity cat bond and as we said, these 2026-4 cat bond notes will sit in a layer above those earlier 2026-2 issuance. With the 2026-2 notes, we were told that an effective first-event attachment equivalent would be at around $600 million for the Class A notes and $1.6 billion for the Class AA’s. We’re told that for the Series 2026-4 Class AAA notes, the effective first-event attachment would be higher at $1.9 billion, directly over the 2026-2 AA tranche. Which shows SafePoint layering efficient reinsurance from the capital markets across a growing share of its reinsurance tower this year, as the company looks to capitalise on cat bond pricing to lock-in multi-year protection that will give the firm meaningful certainty on its reinsurance for the coming years. Strategically that is a sound move at this stage in the cycle, as predicting the length or depth of the soft market is particularly challenging given the volatile global environment seen today and the uncertainty of how a spate of meaningful catastrophe losses could affect reinsurance investor appetites. This now marks the seventh cat bond offering under the Nature Coast Re Ltd. special purpose insurer, and SafePoint’s twelfth cat bond sponsorship overall. You can read all about SafePoint’s cat bonds in our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . You can read all about this new Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-4) catastrophe bond from SafePoint as well as details on almost every cat bond issued in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: Kim Declares Victory in California Insurance Commissioner Race Article 0 Comments Jane Kim claimed victory over fellow Democrat Ben Allen in the race for California insurance commissioner on Friday. Kim was up by more than 400,000 votes as of Friday afternoon. As of Wednesday morning, 99.8% of precincts had reported in, though a large number of votes remain uncounted. Kim had 52.7% of the vote to Allen’s 47.3%. The spread has continued to grow in Kim’s favor in recent days. On Tuesday, Kim had led by 265,000 votes . “Insurance was created as a shared promise. We pay into the system so that when the worst happens, we’re protected,” Kim said in a statement. “Californians have kept our end of that bargain, but insurance companies have broken their side of the promise by denying, delaying and underpaying valid claims and dropping coverage.” Jane Kim Following Kim’s victory declaration, Allen’s campaign released the following statement: “Earlier today, I called Jane Kim to congratulate her. Jane ran a strong race, and it appears that she has won. Assuming that is the case, I desperately want her to succeed, because if she succeeds, the state succeeds – especially the families in need that we’ve been fighting for across the state.” Kim and Allen advanced to the primary in the race for insurance commissioner. The top two together garnered more than 45% of the votes cast in the June 2 primary. The winner replaces outgoing commissioner Ricardo Lara, who is term limited. Kim was pushing a publicly backed single-payer disaster insurance system. Ben Allen Allen is a state Legislator who has authored several bills to address insurance affordability in the state, including creating new home-hardening incentives. The American Property Casualty Insurance Association issued a statement congratulating Kim. “We congratulate Jane Kim on her election as California’s next Insurance Commissioner and look forward to working together to address the state’s ongoing insurance crisis,” the statement, from APCIA’s Denni Ritter, department vice president for state government relations. “While recent reforms are beginning to stabilize the market, the insurance crisis is far from over, and a full recovery will take time. Protecting this progress is critical. Costly new mandates or regulatory actions that drive up costs or limit coverage options risk reversing this progress and worsening the crisis. Insurers remain committed to working with Commissioner-elect Kim, Governor-elect Becerra and Legislative leaders to restore a stable market and ensure every Californian has access to the coverage they need to protect their homes, cars and small businesses.” Topics California Was this article valuable?
